---
title: "Getting started with DBinventory"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

DBinventory answers two questions about a database you have `SELECT` access
to and no documentation for: *what is in it* (the inventory) and *what does
each column hold* (the column profile). This article walks through both on
the 5% sample of the [Fake NHS Trust synthetic
dataset](https://github.com/ThomUK/synthetic-hospital-data), read through its
`fakehospdata` package: about 3.6 million rows in the `layer1`, `reference`,
`derived` and `aggregate` schemas. Its `answers` schema (the mess log and the
truth tables the derived layer is marked against) is the dataset's answer key
rather than part of the trust's warehouse, so the examples exclude it.

```{r setup}
library(DBinventory)
```

## Connect

`db_connect()` takes whatever you have: a DBI connection, an ODBC connection
string or DSN for SQL Server, a SQLite or DuckDB file, or a Parquet file or
directory. `fakehospdata::fh_connect()` downloads the sample once into a cache
and returns a DuckDB connection of views, which `db_connect()` passes through.

```{r connect}
con <- db_connect(fakehospdata::fh_connect("sample", quiet = TRUE))
db_dialect(con)
```

On a hospital warehouse it would be:

```{r mssql, eval = FALSE}
con <- db_connect("Driver={ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server};Server=warehouse;Database=DW;Trusted_Connection=yes;TrustServerCertificate=yes;")
```

## Inventory

`db_inventory()` lists every table and view, every column with its type, and
adds exact row counts, sizes from system views where available, and the
newest value in any date or datetime column as a freshness signal. Regular
expressions on `schema.table` narrow the scope.

```{r inventory}
inv <- db_inventory(con, schema = c("layer1", "reference"), progress = FALSE)
inv$tables[, c("table_schema", "table_name", "n_columns", "row_count", "newest_datetime", "newest_datetime_column")]
```

Columns carry a `type_class` that normalises engine type names, which is what
decides which statistics the profiler can ask for.

```{r columns}
inv$columns[inv$columns$table_name == "pas_patients", c("column_name", "data_type", "type_class")]
```

## Column profile

`db_profile()` runs one aggregate query per table (batched by column) plus one
frequency query per column that has few enough distinct values for a
frequency table to mean something. Tables above `sample_rows` are profiled on
a sample materialised in a temporary table; here that threshold is set low so
the audit logs are sampled.

```{r profile}
prof <- db_profile(con, inv, sample_rows = 2e5, progress = FALSE)
table(prof$sampled)
prof[prof$table_name == "pas_patients",
     c("column_name", "null_rate", "distinct_count", "is_unique", "pk_candidate", "semantic_type", "values_suppressed")]
```

Literal values are suppressed by default for identifiers, free text and
columns whose names suggest personal data, because the profile of a hospital
warehouse will end up in a repository. Codes and dates keep theirs:

```{r top}
top_values_of(prof, "pas_patients", "ethnicity")
prof[prof$column_name == "dob", c("min_value", "max_value")]
```

The hashes are computed before suppression, so copies of a suppressed column
in other tables still match on fingerprint:

```{r dupes}
inv2 <- db_inventory(con, include = c("layer1\\.pas_outpatient_appointments", "derived\\.op_appointments", "reference\\."), progress = FALSE)
prof2 <- db_profile(con, inv2, sample_rows = 2e5, progress = FALSE)
duplicate_candidates(prof2)[, c("n_tables", "columns")]
```

## Foreign key candidates

Every string, integer or uuid column is scored against the `pk_candidate`
columns of the other tables on name, value range and cardinality. The best
target above a confidence threshold becomes `fk_target`. It is a shortlist for
the key register's match-rate tests, not a confirmed relationship.

```{r fks}
prof2[prof2$fk_candidate, c("table_name", "column_name", "fk_target", "fk_confidence", "fk_evidence")]
```

## Store, resume and report

For a warehouse of hundreds of tables, use `inventory_run()`. It writes the
inventory and each table's profile to a SQLite store as it goes, so an
interrupted run resumes where it stopped, and it can export CSV or Parquet and
render the HTML report at the end.

```{r run, eval = FALSE}
out <- inventory_run(
  "Driver={ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server};Server=warehouse;Database=DW;Trusted_Connection=yes;",
  store = "dw_inventory.sqlite",
  export_dir = "dw_inventory_csv",
  report = "dw_inventory.html"
)
```

```{r disconnect}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```
